148.title: Maha Shivaratri (the night vigil)
148.hook: the night is split into four watches, and something is poured over the lingam in each one
148.carry: four doors, opened one at a time
148.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus fast, keep a vigil through the four watches of the night, bathe the Shiva lingam with water, milk, yogurt, ghee or honey, offer bilva leaves, and chant Om Namah Shivaya until dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesh Chaturthi's goodbye: the clay given back to the water, and come early next year. Your line was the goodbye is love.

An all-nighter has a shape. Students cramming for an exam know it, new parents know it, nurses on the night shift know it. The buzz around eleven. The slump at two. A strange clear stretch around four. And the gray light that feels like a reward. On Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva, whole temples keep that shape on purpose, with no deadline at all. You heard the hunter's story on day eighty-three, the man who stayed awake in a tree by accident. Today, how the night is kept on purpose, watch by watch.
screen: `AN ALL-NIGHTER HAS A SHAPE.` → `A WHOLE TEMPLE, ON PURPOSE.` → `WATCH BY WATCH.`

segments.voice: Maha means great. Shiva, the auspicious one. Ratri, night. It falls on the fourteenth night of the waning moon in late winter, the darkest night before the new moon. The day begins with a fast: many eat nothing, or only fruit and milk. At sunset the vigil starts, and it has a shape. The night is divided into four watches, called praharas, each about three hours long. In many temples and homes there's a worship in each watch: the lingam is bathed, and in some traditions each watch gets its own offering. Water, or milk, or yogurt, or ghee, or honey. It's called abhisheka, and it's the heart of the night: pouring, slowly, while chanting. Then bilva leaves, three to a stem, laid on top. Between the watches, people sing, read stories of Shiva, and chant the mantra from mantra week, its five syllables na-mah-shi-vaa-ya, usually with Om before them: Om Namah Shivaya. Some count it on beads through the whole night. Staying awake like this is called jagarana, keeping awake. Here's what the four watches do. A whole night is too big to hold. Four watches of three hours, each with one thing to pour, are just about possible. The night stops being a wall and becomes four doors, each opened in turn. At dawn, people bathe, make a last offering, and break the fast. Some who keep the vigil say the last watch, just before sunrise, is the clearest part of the night.
screen: `MAHA, SHIVA, RATRI.` · `A FAST, THEN SUNSET.` · `FOUR WATCHES, FOUR POURINGS.` · `JAGARANA: KEEPING AWAKE.` · then, large: `A NIGHT BECOMES FOUR DOORS.`

segments.voice: Split this sit into four, the way the night is split: first, just arrive; second, picture water poured slowly over a smooth stone, and let your breath pour out the same way. Third is the slump: when your mind drifts, and it will, just come back; fourth, sit very still, as if the gray light of dawn were just starting. If you pray, you can say Om Namah Shivaya once in each watch.
Maha Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva, kept awake in four watches, with water poured over the lingam until dawn.
Your line: four doors, opened one at a time. Nobody holds the whole night at once. Day one hundred forty-eight.

149.title: Maha Shivaratri (the night vigil)
149.hook: a pillar of fire with no top and no bottom, a swan flying up, a boar digging down, and a flower that told a lie
149.howItsDone: Many Hindus remember the Lingodbhava, Shiva appearing from an endless pillar of light, on Maha Shivaratri; temples often show it carved on the back wall of the shrine, devotees keep the night's vigil before the lingam, and the twelve jyotirlinga temples draw crowds through the night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maha Shivaratri as it's kept: a fast, four watches, water poured, the mantra until dawn. Your line was four doors, opened one at a time.

Brahma and Vishnu are arguing over who matters more when a column of fire bursts up between them, with no top and no bottom. Vishnu becomes a boar and digs down. Brahma becomes a swan and flies up. Neither finds an end, and Vishnu comes back and says so. You heard that on day ninety. Tonight, look again at two things. A small, sweet-smelling flower, drifting down out of the dark. And the pillar, which didn't stay in the story. People say it came down to earth in places you can still visit.
screen: `A PILLAR WITH NO END.` → `A FLOWER DRIFTING DOWN.` → `A PILLAR YOU CAN VISIT.`

segments.voice: In the Shiva Purana's telling, the flower has a name: ketaki, the fragrant screwpine blossom. Brahma, worn out and empty-handed, meets it falling from far above, and asks a favor. Back me up. The flower agrees. Brahma returns and claims he reached the top, and the ketaki says yes, I saw him there. Then the pillar opens and Shiva steps out. Vishnu, who admitted his limit, is honored. Brahma is rebuked, and the story says that's why so few temples are built for him. The flower gets its own sentence: never to be offered in Shiva's worship. Many temples still leave it out. Notice who the story bothers to punish: not only the one who lied, but the witness who said yes to something it never saw. The pillar is the jyotirlinga: jyotis, light, and linga, a sign. Hindus speak of twelve jyotirlinga shrines across India, places where Shiva is said to have shown himself as that light: Somnath on the Gujarat coast, Kashi Vishwanath in Varanasi, Kedarnath high in the Himalayas, Rameshwaram in the far south, and eight more. On Maha Shivaratri their lines run through the night. In many South Indian Shiva temples, the scene is carved on the shrine's back wall: Shiva in the pillar, a swan above, a boar below. This is a Shaiva story, told by Shiva's devotees; Vaishnava Hindus tell their own stories, where Vishnu is the source, and Hindus hold these side by side. Day ninety honored the one who said I don't know. Tonight honors its twin: don't vouch for what you didn't see.

segments.voice: Think of something you passed on lately, a bit of news, a claim about someone, a story you repeated as if you'd seen it, and hold it up gently, like the ketaki in Brahma's hand. Ask, with no blame: did I see this, or did I just say yes? Sort it, seen or heard, then rest in what you actually know.
Maha Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva, which many say remembers the pillar of light that had no end.
Your line: no flower, no bluff. Seen is not the same as heard. Day one hundred forty-nine, done.

150.title: Raksha Bandhan (the thread)
150.hook: a plate with a lamp, red powder, rice, a sweet and a thread; the order you use them in is the ritual
150.howItsDone: On the full moon of Shravan, many Hindu sisters perform a small arti for their brothers, apply a tilak, tie a rakhi on the wrist and feed them a sweet, and brothers give a gift and a promise of protection; today rakhis are also tied between sisters, cousins and friends.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maha Shivaratri's pillar of light: a swan, a boar, a lying flower, and the one who said I couldn't find the end. Your line was no flower, no bluff.

On the full-moon morning of the month of Shravan, in the monsoon, a sister sets down a small steel plate. On it: a little oil lamp, a pinch of red powder, a few grains of rice, one sweet, and a thread. Sometimes a plain red-and-gold string, sometimes a plastic cartoon character her little brother will insist on wearing to school. Her brother sits facing her. Nobody needs instructions. They've done this every year since they were small. But there's an order to it, and the order is the whole ritual.
screen: `A STEEL PLATE, FIVE THINGS.` → `A SISTER, A BROTHER.` → `THE ORDER IS THE RITUAL.`

segments.voice: Here's how it goes in many homes. First the lamp is lit, and the sister circles it before her brother's face, a small arti. Then the tilak: red powder on his forehead, with a few grains of rice pressed into it. Then the thread, tied on his right wrist, with a knot or three. Then the sweet, placed in his mouth. Then his turn: a gift, and a promise to protect her. Raksha, protection. Bandhan, a bond. On days eighty-four and ninety-one you heard where the thread's stories come from: Draupadi tearing her sari to bind Krishna's cut finger, and Indra's wife tying a thread on him before battle. Today, look at the full moon itself, because the rakhi isn't the only thing tied on it. In many South Indian families, men who wear the sacred thread across the chest change it for a new one that morning, a day called Avani Avittam. On the coast of Maharashtra, fishing families offer coconuts to the sea, asking it to be gentle for the season. So Raksha Bandhan isn't really one custom. It's a full moon when people tie things: to each other, to the sea, to their own promises. And today, many sisters tie rakhis on sisters, cousins on cousins, friends on friends, and some people tie one on a tree they've promised to look after. Protection turns out to run in every direction.

The little lamp circles once before your face, a touch of red on your forehead, a thread pulled snug on your wrist with one knot, a sweet. Stay there a few breaths, the one being protected, and if you'd like, thank them silently.
Raksha Bandhan. The bond of protection, tied on the full moon of Shravan with a lamp, a tilak, a thread and a sweet.
Your line: protection runs in every direction. Sometimes yours is the wrist that gets the thread. One hundred fifty days now.

151.title: Makar Sankranti (kites; the sun turns)
151.hook: a whole city on its rooftops, the sky full of kites, and an old warrior on a bed of arrows waiting for the sun to turn
151.howItsDone: On Makar Sankranti, in mid-January, many Hindus bathe in rivers, give to those in need, share sweets of sesame and jaggery, and in Gujarat and elsewhere spend the day flying kites from rooftops to mark the sun's turn north.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raksha Bandhan: lamp, tilak, thread, sweet. Your line was protection runs in every direction.

In mid-January, go to Ahmedabad at sunrise and look up. Every rooftop in the old city has people on it. Families, grandparents on plastic chairs, kids with spools of string. And the sky is full of kites, paper diamonds in every color, tugging, dipping, fighting. Somebody's string cuts somebody else's, and a whole neighborhood yells the same word at once. Food comes up the stairs all day. By night there are paper lanterns floating up. It's called Uttarayan here. Elsewhere, the day is Makar Sankranti. And under all the noise, it's about the sun.
screen: `EVERY ROOFTOP FULL.` → `A SKY FULL OF KITES.` → `UNDER THE NOISE, THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Diwali, Holi and Shivaratri follow the moon, so their dates wander around the calendar from year to year. Makar Sankranti follows the sun, so it lands on almost the same day every year, in mid-January. Sankranti means crossing, the sun moving from one sign of the zodiac into the next. Makara is the sign called Capricorn, so this is the day the sun crosses into Makara. It also marks the start of what the tradition calls uttarayana, the sun's northward journey, the half of the year when the days grow longer. And that turn matters in a famous story. In the Mahabharata, the great-uncle Bhishma falls in battle, shot with so many arrows that he lies on them like a bed, his body never touching the ground. He has a boon: he can choose the moment of his death. And he chooses to wait. For weeks he lies there, teaching, until the sun turns north, because uttarayana was held to be an auspicious time to leave the world. Only then does he let go. So why kites? People give different answers. It's a way of spending the whole day outdoors, in the winter sun, after the cold. Some say the kites are thanks sent up toward the sun. Some just say it's what this day looks like. The texts don't mention kites; the rooftops do. A festival about the sun turning, and a whole city spends the day with its face turned up.
screen: `THE MOON WANDERS, THE SUN DOESN'T.` · `SANKRANTI: THE SUN CROSSES.` · `BHISHMA WAITS FOR THE TURN.` · `THE TEXTS DON'T MENTION KITES.` · then, large: `A WHOLE CITY, FACES TURNED UP.`

segments.voice: If you can, sit where there's a window or real daylight; if not, picture winter sun on your face, and tilt your chin up slightly, the way you would on a rooftop watching a kite. Feel the light on your forehead, your eyelids, your cheeks; the days are getting longer, or they will be. Breathe in, as if you could take in some of that warmth, breathe out slowly, and let your shoulders drop like a string going slack.
Makar Sankranti. The day the sun crosses into Makara, the start of its northward turn, kept with kites and a face turned up.
Your line: a face turned up. The sun has started north. Day one hundred fifty-one, done.

152.title: Makar Sankranti (kites; the sun turns)
152.hook: a small sesame sweet pressed into your palm, and a line that comes with it: take this, and speak sweetly
152.carry: something sweet, something clean, something given
152.howItsDone: On Makar Sankranti many Hindus bathe at dawn in a river, give food, grain or blankets to those in need, and share sweets of sesame and jaggery; the day is kept as Lohri, Bhogali Bihu, Khichdi and Pongal in different regions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Makar Sankranti from the rooftops: the sun crossing into Makara, Bhishma waiting for the turn, a sky full of kites. Your line was a face turned up. Today, the same day, from the kitchen and the riverbank.

In Maharashtra on Sankranti, people go visiting with a little box of sweets: tiny hard balls of sesame and jaggery, the dark unrefined sugar. You hand one to your neighbor and say the line that goes with it: til-gul ghya, god god bola. Take this sesame and jaggery, and speak sweetly. It's a small thing that carries a lot. Maybe you and that neighbor had words over the parking this year. Maybe your aunt said something at the wedding. The sweet is a reset.
screen: `A LITTLE BOX OF SESAME SWEETS.` → `TAKE THIS, AND SPEAK SWEETLY.` → `A RESET.`

segments.voice: Three things turn up again and again on this day. First, sesame: til, in Hindi. In the cold of January, sesame and jaggery are thought of as warming, heavy, good winter food, and today they become sweets: laddus, brittle, little balls handed from house to house. They come with words. Sesame is small and sticks together; jaggery is sweet. So the sweet is a promise about your speech for the year. Second, the river. People bathe at dawn on Sankranti, in the Ganga if they can, or any river, or just at home before sunrise. At Ganga Sagar, where the Ganga meets the sea in Bengal, huge crowds gather to bathe on this day. Water at a winter dawn is cold, and that's part of it: a clean start as the sun turns. Third, giving. Dana, a gift given freely. Sankranti is one of the days when giving is said to count most: sesame, blankets, grain, food for someone who needs it. And the surprise: the same day has many names. In Punjab, the night before, it's Lohri, with bonfires. In Assam, Bhogali Bihu, a harvest feast. In parts of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, people eat khichdi, rice and lentils cooked together, and some even call the day Khichdi. In Tamil Nadu, it's Pongal, and that's tomorrow. One sun, crossing once, and each place meets it with its own food and its own words. Underneath, the pattern holds: something sweet, something clean, something given.

153.title: Pongal / Onam (regional; harvest)
153.hook: a new clay pot of rice and milk set in the sun, and a whole family waiting for it to boil over
153.carry: more than the pot can hold
153.howItsDone: Over four days in the Tamil month of Thai, many Tamil Hindus clear out old things on Bhogi, boil new rice with milk and jaggery until it overflows and offer it to the sun on Thai Pongal, honor their cattle on Mattu Pongal, and visit family on Kaanum Pongal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Makar Sankranti from the kitchen: sesame and sweet words, a cold river, a gift given freely. Your line was something sweet, something clean, something given. Today, Tamil Nadu, and a pot meant to overflow.

Milk on a stove rises, foams and spills over the side, and the cook lunges for the knob too late. In a kitchen, that's a small disaster. In a courtyard in Tamil Nadu in the middle of January, it's the whole point. A brand-new clay pot, a turmeric plant tied around its neck, sits on a little fire in the open sun. Rice, milk and jaggery inside. The whole family stands around it. They're waiting for it to boil over. And when it does, they shout.
screen: `THE MILK BOILS OVER.` → `A NEW CLAY POT IN THE SUN.` → `WAITING FOR IT TO SPILL.`

segments.voice: They shout Pongalo Pongal! Pongal means boiling over. It's the name of the dish, the sweet rice, and of the festival, Tamil Nadu's great harvest festival, in the Tamil month of Thai, on the same days as Makar Sankranti. The rice has just come in from the fields. The overflowing pot is abundance you can see: more than the pot can hold. Pongal runs four days, and each has a job. Day one, Bhogi: clear out the old. Families clean the house, and in many places old things go on a bonfire at dawn. Day two, Thai Pongal, the big day. A kolam, a pattern drawn in rice flour, is laid at the door. The pot boils over in the sun, and the first pongal is offered to Surya, the sun, before anyone eats. Day three, Mattu Pongal, for the cattle. The cows and bulls who plowed the fields are bathed, their horns painted, bells and garlands put on them, and they're fed pongal too: a whole day to thank the animals who did the work. Day four, Kaanum Pongal, for visiting family and friends, and outings. A Tamil saying for this week: Thai piranthal vazhi pirakkum. When Thai is born, a way will be born. A new month, and a new road opens. A harvest festival, and a very complete way of saying thank you.
screen: `PONGAL MEANS BOILING OVER.` · `BHOGI: CLEAR OUT THE OLD.` · `THE SUN, THEN THE CATTLE.` · `WHEN THAI IS BORN, A WAY IS BORN.` · then, large: `MORE THAN THE POT CAN HOLD.`

segments.voice: Walk through the four days in your mind: one old thing you're ready to put on the fire, a habit, a grudge, a drawer of junk, and one thing that simply gave you life this week, like light, food or sleep. Then silently thank someone who does the hard work so you can eat, earn or rest and rarely hears it, and name one person you'd like to go and see. 154.title: Pongal / Onam (regional; harvest)
154.hook: a flower carpet that grows every morning for ten days, because a beloved king is coming home to check on his people
154.howItsDone: During the ten days of Onam in the Malayalam month of Chingam, many Hindus in Kerala lay a pookalam of flowers at the door that grows each day, wear new clothes, and share the Onam sadhya on banana leaves to welcome King Mahabali on his yearly visit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pongal: a new pot boiling over in the sun, and four days of thank-yous, cattle included. Your line was more than the pot can hold. Today, the other harvest, in Kerala, and a look back at the week.
screen: `PONGAL: MORE THAN THE POT CAN HOLD.`

segments.voice: In Kerala, in late summer, on the first morning of Onam, someone gets up early and lays a small circle of flower petals at the front door. Yellow, orange, white. Next morning, it grows a ring. And the next. For ten days it grows, a carpet of flowers called a pookalam, until by the last day it's a whole bright mandala across the doorstep. Why the trouble? A guest is coming. Not a god this time. A king, and he wants to see that his people are happy.
screen: `A CIRCLE OF PETALS AT THE DOOR.` → `BIGGER EVERY MORNING FOR TEN DAYS.` → `A KING IS COMING.`

segments.voice: The king is Mahabali, an asura, from the side of the story usually cast as the gods' rivals. But in Kerala he's remembered as the best king there ever was. A Malayalam folk song still sung at Onam remembers his reign as a time when all people were equal: no lies, no cheating, no one poor. The gods grew worried about how powerful he'd become. So Vishnu came to him as Vamana, a small boy-priest, and asked for just as much land as he could cover in three steps. Bali, who never refused anyone, said yes. And the boy grew. One step covered the earth. The second, the heavens. There was nowhere left for the third, so Bali bowed and offered his own head. Vamana's foot pressed him down into the world below. The Bhagavata Purana tells it as a story of Bali's devotion and generosity: he's rewarded, not destroyed. Kerala adds something: Bali asked to visit his people once a year. Onam is that visit, so everyone makes sure he'll find them well. The pookalam. New clothes. The Onam sadhya, a huge vegetarian feast on a banana leaf, often more than twenty dishes, eaten together. Boat races on the backwaters. It's Kerala's harvest festival too, in the month of Chingam. And that's the week: Shivaratri's four watches and its pillar of light, Raksha Bandhan's thread, the sun turning at Sankranti, Pongal's pot, and a king coming home. Different stories, same instinct: make the day worth arriving for.
screen: `AN ASURA, THE BEST OF KINGS.` · `THREE STEPS: EARTH, HEAVEN, HIS HEAD.` · `ONE VISIT A YEAR: ONAM.` · `THE WEEK: VIGIL, THREAD, SUN, POT.` · then, large: `MAKE THE DAY WORTH ARRIVING FOR.`

segments.voice: Imagine Mahabali is visiting you this year, not to judge, just to see how you are. For each thing that's good in your life right now, lay one ring of petals at your door, and let the circle grow without rushing it. When it's full, sit beside it like someone waiting for a guest they love.
Pongal and Onam. Two harvests: Tamil Nadu's pot boiling over for the sun, and Kerala's flower carpet for a king who comes home once a year.
Your line: worth arriving for. A week of festivals, behind you. That's day one hundred fifty-four.
